title: Hadoop to the lakehouse
tagline: Two companies started at opposite ends of the same problem — one from open files and an open engine, one from a closed managed warehouse — and spent a decade walking toward each other.

events.title: GFS and MapReduce
events.summary: Two papers argue that a pile of cheap, unreliable machines can process a web's worth of data, as long as the framework absorbs the failures.

media.alt: Parallel map lanes converge on one reduce result, with a failed task replaced

keyPoints: GFS (2003) splits files into large replicated blocks across commodity disks.
MapReduce (2004) gives the programmer two functions, map and reduce; the framework does the parallelism, scheduling, and retries.
Intermediate results are written to disk between stages, so a lost machine costs one task, not the job.
Move the computation to where the data already sits, rather than the data to the computation.
events.impact: Made large-scale data processing something a company without Google's infrastructure team could imagine doing. The price was latency: every stage ends in a disk write, which is the gap Spark was built to close.

resources.label: MapReduce: Simplified Data Processing on Large Clusters

events.title: Hadoop
events.summary: The papers become open source: HDFS for storage and MapReduce for compute, running on racks of ordinary servers.

media.alt: Four connected server racks each hold disks and a processor

keyPoints: Grew out of the Nutch web crawler; Yahoo's investment turned it into a platform.
HDFS for storage, MapReduce for compute, later YARN to schedule both.
Schema-on-read: land the data first, decide what it means later.
Storage and compute lived on the same machines, so growing one meant buying the other.
events.impact: Set the shape of the big-data decade, including its habits: tightly coupled clusters, hand-written Java jobs, and lakes that quietly turned into swamps.

events.title: Hive and the Metastore
events.summary: Analysts write SQL; Hive compiles it into MapReduce jobs. The part that outlived the engine was the catalogue that remembered what the files meant.

media.alt: A table linked to a metastore card, with files suggested behind it

keyPoints: HiveQL: a SQL dialect that spares analysts from writing Java.
The Hive Metastore stores table names, schemas, partitions, and file locations.
Later added faster engines (Tez, LLAP), a cost-based optimiser, and ACID tables on ORC.
Spark SQL, Presto/Trino, and Athena all still read the Hive Metastore.
events.impact: Showed that a declarative layer comes back to any new storage substrate within a few years. Hive's execution engine faded; its SQL dialect and its Metastore are still everywhere.

resources.label: Choosing a data platform by workload

events.title: Spark and the RDD
events.byline: Zaharia et al., UC Berkeley AMPLab
events.summary: Keep the working set in memory between steps, and recover lost pieces by replaying how they were made instead of copying them to disk.

media.alt: Partitioned stages in memory, with a lost tile recovered through lineage

keyPoints: Started in 2009 at Berkeley and open-sourced in 2010, to speed up iterative and interactive jobs that MapReduce handled badly.
A Resilient Distributed Dataset is an immutable, partitioned collection plus the recipe that produced it.
Lineage replaces replication: a lost partition is recomputed from its parents.
Iterative jobs such as machine learning ran 10-100x faster than on Hadoop, as the paper reported.
events.impact: Turned the disk-to-disk batch model into a memory-first one, and gave one engine room to grow into SQL, streaming, graphs, and ML. The branch below follows it from 2013 to 2023.

events.title: Apache top-level project
events.summary: Spark enters the Apache incubator in 2013 and graduates the following February.

events.title: Spark 1.0 and Spark SQL
events.summary: The first stable API line. Spark SQL takes over from Shark, the earlier Hive-on-Spark.

events.title: GraySort record
events.summary: Sorts 100 TB roughly three times faster than the previous Hadoop record, on about a tenth of the machines.

events.title: Spark 2.0
events.summary: One entry point, DataFrame and Dataset unified, and whole-stage code generation. Structured Streaming arrives as a preview.

events.title: Structured Streaming is stable
events.summary: A stream is an unbounded table queried with the same DataFrame API as a batch job.

events.title: Kubernetes and pandas UDFs
events.summary: Native Kubernetes scheduling, and Arrow-based vectorised pandas UDFs make Python a first-class citizen.

events.title: Adaptive Query Execution
events.summary: The plan is re-optimised at runtime using real shuffle statistics: coalesced partitions, skew-join handling, dynamic partition pruning.

events.title: Spark Connect
events.summary: A thin gRPC protocol separates the client application from the driver, so Spark can be used like a service.

events.title: Databricks
events.byline: Spark's creators, including Ghodsi, Zaharia, Stoica, and Xin
events.summary: The people who built Spark start a company to run it for you as a managed cloud service.

media.alt: A cloud cluster beside a runnable notebook

keyPoints: Open-source engine, commercial platform: notebooks, managed clusters, and a job scheduler on top of Spark.
Cloud-first from the start, so the cluster is something you rent, not something you own.
Broadened into machine learning with MLflow (2018), open-sourced for experiment tracking and a model registry.
Most of its later engine work (Photon, Delta, Unity Catalog) sits underneath Spark's own APIs.
events.impact: Established the pattern of this whole rail: an open project, a company that makes it painless, and a slowly widening gap between what the open version does and what the platform does.

events.title: DataFrames and Catalyst
events.summary: Describe what you want, not how to compute it, and let an optimiser rewrite the plan. The RDD era's "how" becomes SQL's "what".

media.alt: A query plan is simplified by pushing a filter toward the table

keyPoints: Spark 1.3 (March 2015) introduces schema-aware DataFrames.
Catalyst rewrites logical plans with rules: predicate pushdown, column pruning, join reordering.
Project Tungsten adds off-heap binary rows and code generation to approach hardware limits.
DataFrame code and SQL compile to the same plan, so they perform the same.
events.impact: The second of Spark's three big shifts (disk to memory, imperative to declarative, batch cluster to unified platform). It is why PySpark can be fast even though Python is not.

resources.label: Spark SQL: Relational Data Processing in Spark

events.title: Snowflake
events.summary: The opposite bet: a closed, fully managed SQL warehouse designed for the cloud, with storage and compute separated and nothing to tune.

media.alt: Storage, independent compute boxes, and services in three layers

keyPoints: Founded in 2012 by two ex-Oracle architects and the co-creator of the Vectorwise engine; out of stealth in late 2014, generally available in mid-2015.
Three layers: columnar micro-partitions in object storage, independent virtual warehouses, and a cloud-services brain for optimiser, metadata, and transactions.
Zero-copy cloning, Time Travel, and secure data sharing fall out of immutable micro-partitions.
Runs on AWS, Azure, and GCP.
events.impact: Where Spark asked you to operate an engine, Snowflake asked you to write SQL. For a decade the choice between them was really a choice between control and convenience.

events.title: Slootman takes over
events.summary: Frank Slootman becomes CEO and the company turns from a technology into a very large business.

events.title: IPO
events.summary: The largest software IPO to that date, and the point where the warehouse-versus-lakehouse rivalry became public and financial.

events.title: Snowpark
events.summary: A DataFrame API in Python, Java, and Scala that looks like PySpark but runs inside Snowflake.

events.title: Streamlit, Unistore, Iceberg preview
events.summary: Buys Streamlit, announces Hybrid Tables for transactional work, and previews Iceberg Tables.

events.title: Ramaswamy becomes CEO
events.summary: Sridhar Ramaswamy takes over and the product turns toward AI: Cortex functions, the Arctic model, and later agents.

events.title: Delta Lake
events.summary: A transaction log placed beside the Parquet files, so a folder in object storage starts behaving like a table with commits.

media.alt: Data files beside a commit ledger showing an added and removed file

keyPoints: ACID transactions over cloud object storage by appending to an ordered log of table changes.
Schema enforcement and evolution, time travel, and efficient upserts (MERGE).
Streaming and batch read and write the same table.
Open source from 2019, with the rest of the features opened up with Delta Lake 2.0 in 2022.
events.impact: Removed the main reason a warehouse was necessary: reliable updates. It is the technical core of the lakehouse argument that came next.

resources.label: Delta Lake: High-Performance ACID Table Storage over Cloud Object Stores

events.title: The lakehouse and Photon
events.summary: Databricks argues that open lake storage plus warehouse features can replace the two-system architecture, and builds a C++ engine to prove the performance claim.

media.alt: A lake roof over data shelves beside a rising performance chart

keyPoints: Lakehouse: open file formats, a transactional metadata layer, and a fast SQL engine on one copy of the data.
Photon is a proprietary vectorised C++ engine that keeps Spark's APIs and replaces its execution.
Databricks SQL, Unity Catalog, and serverless warehouses follow to present a warehouse-shaped surface.
Spark's JVM execution has been moving toward native engines throughout (Photon, and open projects such as Velox-based Gluten).
events.impact: The first time the lake-side vendor moved up into warehousing, rather than the other way round. It also set up the benchmark fight in 2021.

resources.label: Lakehouse: A New Generation of Open Platforms
Photon: A Fast Query Engine for Lakehouse Systems

events.title: Unity Catalog; Delta 2.0
events.summary: A single place for access control, lineage, and discovery across data and AI assets; the remaining Delta features are open-sourced.

events.title: MosaicML
events.summary: Buys a model-training company and repositions itself from a lakehouse to a Data + AI platform.

events.title: Declarative pipelines go upstream
events.byline: From Delta Live Tables to Apache Spark
events.summary: The core of Delta Live Tables is contributed to Apache Spark and lands as Spark Declarative Pipelines in 4.1.

events.title: The benchmark dispute
events.summary: Databricks claims a warehouse benchmark record; Snowflake publicly disputes the comparison. The two companies are now plainly competitors.

media.alt: Two race bars approach a finish line under a disputed stopwatch

keyPoints: The benchmark was TPC-DS, the standard decision-support workload.
The argument was about methodology: what is compared, on what configuration, at what price.
Both sides published their own numbers, which is the lesson in itself.
Neither company's results should be taken from the vendor's own blog without reading the setup.
events.impact: Marks the moment the two platforms stopped talking past each other. Treat vendor benchmarks as marketing until you have reproduced the setup on your own workload.

events.title: Open formats and the catalog war
events.summary: The fight moves from who owns the compute to who owns the catalog, the thing that decides which engines can see which tables.

media.alt: An open card catalog connects through locks to four engines

keyPoints: Apache Iceberg (from Netflix) and Delta Lake compete as the open table format; Hudi (from Uber) is the third.
June 2024: Databricks buys Tabular, founded by Iceberg's creators, and open-sources Unity Catalog the same week as Snowflake's Summit.
Snowflake launches Polaris, an Iceberg REST catalog, and donates it to Apache.
Interoperability becomes the sales pitch: Delta UniForm, Iceberg REST, and engines reading each other's tables.
events.impact: Customers stop being asked to pick a storage format and start being asked to pick a catalog. Whoever holds the catalog holds governance, lineage, and the default path to the compute.

events.title: Spark 4
events.summary: Spark settles into being a mature SQL engine: ANSI semantics by default, a semi-structured type, pipe syntax, declarative pipelines, and the first real-time mode.

media.alt: Nested blueprint squares with a check mark and semi-structured braces

keyPoints: ANSI SQL mode is on by default: an invalid cast now raises an error instead of quietly returning NULL (use try_cast to get the old behaviour).
A VARIANT type for semi-structured data, SQL pipe syntax, and a Python Data Source API.
4.1 adds Spark Declarative Pipelines and a first Real-Time Mode for Structured Streaming.
Spark Connect becomes a more mature default way to talk to a cluster.
events.impact: Practical consequence for a working engineer: code that relied on silent NULLs will start failing after the upgrade, which is the point. Check the Spark news archive for the current support windows.

events.title: Both buy Postgres
events.summary: Each analytics platform adds an operational database, so the application and the analytics can sit next to each other.

media.alt: Two Postgres databases, each attached to a separate analytics platform

keyPoints: Databricks acquires Neon, and it becomes Lakebase, a serverless Postgres inside the lakehouse.
Snowflake acquires Crunchy Data and ships Snowflake Postgres.
Earlier attempts at this problem were Hybrid Tables and Unistore on the Snowflake side.
The aim is fewer copies and fewer pipelines between where data is written and where it is analysed.
events.impact: OLTP was the last piece neither platform owned. Buying the same open-source database within weeks of each other shows how closely they now watch one another.

events.title: Reyden and Lakehouse//RT
events.summary: A new engine aims to serve millisecond queries directly from Delta and Iceberg tables, without a separate real-time copy.

media.alt: Many packets pass through a narrow channel into dashboard tiles

keyPoints: Named after Reynold Xin ("Reynold's Dream Engine").
Targets real-time dashboards, applications, and high-concurrency AI agents.
Databricks reports roughly 10 ms on small data and under 100 ms at about 12,000 queries per second.
Lineage: MapReduce, Spark on the JVM, Tungsten, Photon, then Reyden.
events.impact: Moves the lakehouse into serving workloads that used to need a separate store. These figures are the vendor's own and the product was in beta when this was written; check the current status before relying on them.

events.title: Where they meet
events.byline: Snowflake Summit 2026, and the state of play
events.summary: Snowflake answers with agents, built-in streaming, adaptive compute, and Iceberg v3. By now the two platforms compete on almost every layer.

media.alt: Coral and blue platform layers connect through a dense network

keyPoints: June 1-4, 2026: more than twenty-five announcements around an "agentic enterprise".
Snowflake Intelligence becomes CoWork, a personal agent, and Cortex Code becomes CoCo, a coding agent.
Datastream adds streaming ingestion, Adaptive Compute reduces manual warehouse sizing, and Iceberg v3 is supported.
Open this entry for the side-by-side comparison and the interview one-liners.
events.impact: Databricks moved down from the lake to the warehouse; Snowflake moved up from the warehouse to the lake. The interesting question for a practitioner is no longer which one, but which trade-offs you are accepting.
